papers.title: Pathological levels of α-synuclein increase basal mitophagy in Parkinson’s dopamine neurons
papers.summary: This paper investigates how elevated levels of α-synuclein, a protein strongly linked to Parkinson's disease, affect mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) in dopamine neurons. The researchers found that pathological α-synuclein levels increase basal mitophagy activity in these neurons, even without additional stress. This suggests that excess α-synuclein may overburden or dysregulate the normal mitochondrial quality control process, potentially contributing to neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: Since the abstract is minimal, the full paper likely contains detailed mitophagy assays and possibly imaging data directly relevant to mitophagy mechanisms in vulnerable neuron populations, which could inform methodological or conceptual approaches for studying interneurons and mitochondrial quality control in the brain.

papers.title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
papers.summary: This study uses a genome-wide CRISPR screen to find genes that control mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria) in dopaminergic neurons independent of the well-known PRKN/Parkin pathway. By systematically knocking out genes across the genome, the researchers identify new regulators that could explain how neurons clear damaged mitochondria even without functional Parkin. These findings help fill a gap in understanding neuronal quality control pathways relevant to Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions.
papers.why: Identifying new, non-canonical mitophagy regulators in neurons directly expands the molecular toolkit relevant to this PhD's focus on mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in brain neurons.

papers.title: Restoration of mitophagy by crebanine suppresses sevoflurane-induced microglial activation and cognitive deficits by blocking mitochondrial DNA-triggered cGAS-STING pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates how sevoflurane, a common anesthetic, causes cognitive problems by activating microglia (brain immune cells) through a pathway involving mitochondrial DNA leakage and the cGAS-STING signaling cascade. The researchers found that a compound called crebanine can restore mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, which prevents this harmful chain of events. By blocking the mitochondrial DNA from triggering the cGAS-STING pathway, crebanine treatment reduced microglial activation and improved cognitive outcomes in the experimental model.
papers.why: This paper's focus on mitophagy restoration as a mechanism to control neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits is directly relevant to understanding mitochondrial quality control pathways in brain cells, which parallels the mitophagy mechanisms being studied in neurons for this PhD project.

papers.title: Nutrients and Their Role in Autophagy Regulation.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how different nutrients, such as amino acids, glucose, and lipids, influence the activation or suppression of autophagy. It likely covers key nutrient-sensing pathways like mTOR and AMPK that respond to cellular energy and nutrient status to regulate autophagic flux. The review probably synthesizes evidence from various cell types and organisms on how dietary and metabolic signals shape autophagy outcomes.
papers.why: Understanding nutrient-driven regulation of autophagy provides mechanistic context for interpreting spatial metabolomics data alongside mitophagy and autophagy markers in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: Apolipoprotein E4 Exacerbates Aβ Oligomer-Induced Synaptotoxicity through Promoting Autophagic Degradation of Glutathione Peroxidase 4
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the ApoE4 genetic variant, a major Alzheimer's risk factor, worsens synaptic damage caused by amyloid-beta oligomers. The mechanism involves ApoE4 promoting autophagic (self-digesting) degradation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key antioxidant enzyme that protects against lipid peroxidation. By depleting GPX4 through autophagy, ApoE4 increases oxidative stress and synaptic vulnerability, linking autophagy dysfunction to Alzheimer's-related synaptotoxicity.
papers.why: This paper connects autophagy-mediated protein degradation to neuronal vulnerability and oxidative stress, offering mechanistic insight relevant to how autophagic pathways shape synaptic and neuronal health in disease contexts studied in the profile.

papers.title: Astragalin ameliorates cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease model mice: Role of the iron metabolism-autophagy axis.
papers.summary: This study examines astragalin, a natural flavonoid compound, and its effects on cognitive decline in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers investigate how astragalin may improve memory and thinking abilities by targeting the connection between iron metabolism and autophagy, the cell's waste-clearing process. The findings suggest that restoring balance in these two interconnected systems could be a therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This paper's focus on the iron metabolism-autophagy axis in neurons is directly relevant to the project's emphasis on mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurodegenerative contexts, offering mechanistic insight that could inform spatial transcriptomic or metabolomic investigations of iron and autophagy markers in brain tissue.

papers.title: Advances in Multidimensional Molecular Mechanisms of Epilepsy and Precision Therapy Strategies.
papers.summary: This paper reviews current understanding of epilepsy across multiple molecular levels, including genetic, epigenetic, and signaling pathway mechanisms. It discusses how these mechanisms interact to drive seizure activity and disease progression. The review also outlines emerging precision medicine approaches aimed at tailoring epilepsy treatment based on individual molecular profiles.
papers.why: Epilepsy involves disrupted neuronal circuits and interneuron dysfunction, making this relevant to understanding interneuron and perineuronal net pathology in excitability disorders that may intersect with mitophagy-related neuronal stress.

papers.title: Streptococcus suis-induced mitophagy via Eno-HSP90AA1 interaction disrupts the blood-brain barrier.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the bacterium Streptococcus suis triggers excessive mitophagy (selective autophagic clearance of mitochondria) in cells of the blood-brain barrier. The researchers identify an interaction between a bacterial protein (Eno) and the host chaperone HSP90AA1 as the trigger for this process. This mitophagy-driven mitochondrial dysfunction weakens the blood-brain barrier, potentially explaining how the bacterium invades the central nervous system.
papers.why: While focused on bacterial infection rather than neuronal biology, this paper offers mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation via protein-protein interactions affecting barrier integrity, which may inform understanding of mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal and glial health in the brain.
